Boeing’s 2022 Form 10-K reports the following revenue recognized on fixed-price contracts:

- **Commercial Airplanes (BCA): 100%**
- **Defense, Space & Security (BDS): 60%**
- **Global Services (BGS): 88%**

These figures appear in Note 22, “Segment and Revenue Information” (pp. 111–112).

As of December 31, 2023, Boeing said approximately **33%** of its workforce—about 57,000 employees—was represented by unions. Its table of principal agreements gives these shares of **all Boeing employees**:

- **21%** — International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM), including Districts 751 and 837.
- **10%** — Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA), Professional and Technical groups.
- **1%** — United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW), District 1069.

The listed union percentages total 32%; the filing separately reports the overall figure as approximately 33%. (Form 10-K, Human Capital, p. 2; labor-risk discussion, p. 9.)

The filing gives four percentages for 2025:

| Share | Amount it applies to |
|---|---|
| **46%** | Boeing’s **total revenue**, attributable to non-U.S. customers, including Foreign Military Sales through the U.S. government. |
| **60%** | **Commercial Airplanes revenue from customer contracts**, attributable to non-U.S. customers. |
| **Approximately 85%** | **Commercial Airplanes’ total backlog, in dollar terms**, associated with non-U.S. airlines. |
| **26%** | **Defense, Space & Security backlog** attributable to non-U.S. customers. |

The first two percentages are stated in the non-U.S. sales discussion; the backlog figures appear in the Commercial Airplanes and Defense, Space & Security sections.

The filing dates these developments to 2025 (Item 3, p. 18; related Google disclosure in Item 1A, p. 14):

- **April 23 — EU DMA investigations:** The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** in the Article 5(4) investigation and ordered it to remove restrictions on steering users to alternatives outside the App Store; Apple appealed. The same day, the Commission issued **preliminary findings** in a separate Article 6(4) investigation into Apple’s contractual requirements for developers and app marketplaces—not a final violation finding.
- **April 30 — Epic Games:** A California federal court found Apple violated the 2021 injunction, barred fees on purchases made outside apps and restrictions on developers steering customers to those purchases, denied Apple’s motion to narrow or vacate the injunction, and referred the matter to the U.S. Attorney to consider criminal-contempt proceedings. Apple appealed.
- **September 2 — Google antitrust case:** A D.C. federal court ordered remedies after finding Google had violated U.S. antitrust law in 2024. The order remained subject to further proceedings and appeals; changes could affect Google’s search-distribution arrangements with Apple.
- **October — Epic appeal:** The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments on an expedited basis in Apple’s appeal of the April 30 ruling.

Apple identified these fiscal 2024 results as unfavorably affected by currency weakness against the U.S. dollar:

- **Greater China net sales:** Weaker **renminbi** was a headwind; sales fell 8% to $66.952 billion.
- **Japan net sales:** Weaker **yen** was a headwind, although sales rose 3% to $25.052 billion.
- **Rest of Asia Pacific net sales:** Weakness in foreign currencies had a net unfavorable impact, although sales rose 4% to $30.658 billion.
- **Products gross margin and gross-margin percentage:** Currency weakness partially offset other factors supporting their increases. Margin rose to $109.633 billion and 37.2%, respectively.

These are the currency effects expressly noted in the MD&A (Form 10-K, pp. 22 and 24).

| Percentage | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **40%** | Fiscal 2025 net sales through Apple’s **direct** distribution channels. |
| **60%** | Fiscal 2025 net sales through Apple’s **indirect** distribution channels. |
| **12%** | One unnamed customer’s share of total **trade receivables** as of September 27, 2025. |
| **34%** | Third-party cellular network carriers’ share of total **trade receivables** on that date. |
| **46% and 23%** | The respective shares of total **vendor non-trade receivables** attributable to two vendors on that date. |

The channel figures are in “Markets and Distribution” (Form 10-K, p. 2); the receivables figures are in “Accounts Receivable” (p. 39). The filing does not say whether the customer representing 12% is part of the carrier group, so those two trade-receivables figures should not be treated as distinct portions to add together.

- **Employees involved:** IAM District 837 represented approximately **3,200 Boeing employees** at its St. Louis-area sites—the group involved in the strike. For context, Boeing separately reported about **182,000 employees** and **72,000 union members** company-wide at December 31, 2025. The table’s **25%** figure is IAM’s share of Boeing’s workforce across districts, not District 837’s share. *(Human Capital, p. 2; MD&A, p. 24.)*
- **Strike:** The filing says it lasted **101 days**, beginning **August 4, 2025**. It ended on **November 13, 2025**, when District 837 employees voted to ratify a new contract. *(MD&A, p. 24; Risk Factors, p. 9.)*
- **Current agreement:** Boeing’s collective-bargaining table lists **IAM District 837, Missouri**, with an expiration of **July 2030**. That is the agreement’s listed expiration—not the strike’s duration. The filing gives no exact day in July, contract start date, or full agreement term. *(Human Capital, p. 2.)*

All amounts are U.S. dollars. Excluding the January 26, 2025 comparative balances:

- **$20.832 billion** — total goodwill carrying balance at **January 25, 2026** (rounded to **$20.8 billion** in Note 5).
- **$20.5 billion** — the portion allocated to the **Compute & Networking** reporting unit.
- **$370 million** — the portion allocated to the **Graphics** reporting unit. These two segment amounts are components of the total balance.
- **$15.6 billion** — goodwill added, in total, during fiscal 2026; NVIDIA says it was allocated to **Compute & Networking**.
- **$14.4 billion** — goodwill recorded in connection with NVIDIA’s December 2025 Groq agreement. NVIDIA says it primarily represents the workforce and future development of the licensed technology; it was recorded in Compute & Networking and is tax deductible. This amount is part of—not in addition to—the $15.6 billion fiscal-year increase. The agreement licensed Groq’s language-processing-unit technology and included hiring certain employees; NVIDIA says it did not purchase Groq’s customer contracts, existing products, or equity interests.

Sources: Consolidated Balance Sheets, p. 53; Notes 2 and 5, pp. 61 and 63.

The 10-K describes these realized or possibly past effects:

- U.S. and other jurisdictions’ sanctions and export controls blocked the passage of NVIDIA products, services, and support into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine. (Item 1A, p. 28)
- During fiscal 2023, NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia and later closed its Russian operations. It noted that direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2022 had been immaterial. (Item 7, p. 37)
- The war had affected end-customer sales in EMEA. (Item 1A, p. 28)
- NVIDIA’s revenue to partners that sell into Russia **may have been** negatively affected by the war. (Item 7, p. 37)

The filing does not quantify these sales effects. I have excluded its forward-looking warning that the EMEA impact might continue.

For fiscal 2024, the 10-K reports:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$2.2 billion** | Total provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations, as reported in the MD&A. |
| **$774 million** | Inventory provision recorded in cost of revenue. The filing’s policy describes inventory provisions as write-downs to lower of cost or net realizable value, or for excess or obsolete inventory; it does not break this figure down by cause. |
| **Approximately $1.4 billion** | Cost-of-revenue expense for inventory purchase obligations above current demand projections, supplier charges, and penalties related to cancellations and underutilization. |
| **$540 million** | Provision release from sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations. The filing does not split the release between those sources. |

The $774 million and approximately $1.4 billion disclosures roughly reconcile to the rounded $2.2 billion total; they are not amounts to add on top of that total. (MD&A, p. 40; Note 10, pp. 68, 70; inventory policy, p. 37.)

In the **non-exhibit portions** of Boeing’s 2024 Form 10-K, the distinct dividend amounts are:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **Up to $345 million per year** | Boeing’s estimate of the annual **cash** it might need for preferred-stock dividends through October 15, 2027. It is a projected liquidity need, not a dividend declared or paid for 2024. (Risk Factors, p. 17) |
| **$58 million** | Dividends **accumulated during 2024**, shown as a deduction in calculating the loss attributable to common shareholders and in the EPS calculation. It is not the $72 million cash payment below. (Consolidated Statements of Operations, p. 54; Note 4, p. 73) |
| **$72 million** | Dividends declared in December 2024 for holders of record on January 1, 2025, and **paid in cash on January 15, 2025**. (Note 19, p. 106; also shown in the Statements of Equity, p. 58) |
| **$12.50 per share** | The per-share amount the filing associates with the **$72 million declaration**—not an additional dividend amount. (Note 19, p. 106) |

The filing repeats the $58 million and $72 million in financial-statement presentations; each is counted once here.

The filing gives the following ownership levels:

| Pfizer’s Haleon ownership | When it applied |
|---|---|
| **32%** | As of **December 31, 2023** |
| **Approximately 23%** | After the **March 2024** sale; the filing refers to the reduction from about 32% to 23% in its discussion of first-quarter 2024 dividends |
| **Approximately 15%** | After the **October 2024** sale; as of **December 31, 2024** |
| **Approximately 7%** | After an additional sale in **first-quarter 2025** |

The 32%, 23%, and 15% figures appear in Note 2C; the 7% figure appears in the MD&A capital-allocation discussion (Form 10-K, pp. 66 and 47).

As of **January 31, 2022**, the filing gives these counts:

| Business segment | Pickup locations | Delivery locations |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Walmart U.S.** | **Approximately 4,600** | **More than 3,500 same-day delivery locations** |
| **Walmart International** | **Approximately 2,900** | **Over 1,900** |

The U.S. figures are stated in the segment’s omni-channel discussion; International’s are stated alongside its pickup and delivery services. The filing does **not** label the International delivery count as same-day. *(Form 10-K, Item 1, “Walmart U.S. Segment,” p. 7; “Walmart International Segment,” p. 9.)*

The filing gives these related but distinct figures:

- **Approximately $700 million** — costs Pfizer expected to incur in connection with separating Upjohn. Of that, **approximately 75%** had been incurred from inception through December 31, 2021. The charges included costs and expenses related to separating legal entities and transaction costs. *(MD&A, p. 26.)*
- **$434 million in 2020** and **$83 million in 2019** — separation-related costs Pfizer incurred in those years. They were included in “Discontinued operations—net of tax” and primarily related to professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities in finance, tax, legal and information-system functions, as well as investment-banking fees. *(Note 2B, p. 65.)*

Amounts are in **$ millions**. The filing’s fiscal 2025 amounts are:

| Investment type | Gain/(loss) | What it represents |
|---|---:|---|
| Publicly held equity securities | **+$163** | Net unrealized gains for fiscal 2025 on investments held at period-end. This is a fiscal-year amount, not the cumulative year-end holding gain. |
| Publicly held equity securities | **+$88** | Net realized gains on securities sold—the difference between sale proceeds and carrying value at the start of the period, or at purchase if acquired later. |
| Non-marketable equity securities | **+$816** | Unrealized gains recognized during fiscal 2025. |
| Non-marketable equity securities | **−$59** | Impairments and unrealized losses recognized during fiscal 2025. |
| Non-marketable equity securities | **+$565** | A fourth-quarter unrealized gain from a secondary equity transaction in one private-company investment; it is part of the **$816 million**, not an additional gain. |

**Calculated totals:** publicly held securities, **+$251 million**; non-marketable securities, **+$757 million**; combined, **+$1,008 million**. The filing does not state that combined total as a separate line. The gains and losses are recognized in “Other income (expense), net”; I have excluded the total of that line, as well as the cumulative year-end holding amounts and fiscal 2024 figures.

Source: NVIDIA fiscal 2025 Form 10-K, Note 7 (p. 66), Note 8 (pp. 68–69), and accounting policies (pp. 60, 68).

The filing specifically quantifies affiliate borrowings for two operating businesses:

- **Clayton Homes:** Borrowings from Berkshire finance affiliates **increased by $6.6 billion** in 2024, reaching **$24.3 billion at year-end**. (MD&A, K-48)
- **Pilot Travel Centers:** Borrowed **$5.7 billion** from Berkshire insurance subsidiaries in March 2024 to repay third-party debt, then repaid **$1.0 billion** of the affiliate borrowing during the year. (MD&A, K-53; Note 19, K-99)

The Pilot figures imply about **$4.7 billion** remained from that advance, but the filing does not separately state that as a year-end affiliate-loan balance.

The filing gives these qualifying balances as of December 31, 2023 (USD):

| Amount | What it represents | Filing reference |
|---|---|---|
| **$21.404 billion** | PTC segment’s identifiable assets at year-end | Note 26, p. K-114 |
| **$6.605 billion** | PTC segment goodwill at year-end, reported separately from identifiable assets | Note 26, p. K-114 |
| **Approximately $6.6 billion** | Net carrying value of other intangible assets related to PTC | Note 13, p. K-91 |
| **$5.776 billion** | Notes payable and other borrowings of PTC and its subsidiaries | Note 19, p. K-102 |
| **Approximately $2.1 billion** | Receivables related to PTC within the railroad, utilities and energy businesses | Note 8, p. K-88 |
| **Approximately $1.7 billion** | Inventories, materials and supplies attributable to PTC within those businesses | Note 9, p. K-89 |

The receivables, inventory and intangible-asset amounts are components of broader asset balances, not amounts to add to the **$21.404 billion** of segment identifiable assets. I excluded combined balances without a separately stated PTC amount, as well as 2023 flows and acquisition-date figures.

As of January 31, 2026, Walmart reported these amounts for the receive-fixed-rate, pay-fixed-rate cross-currency swaps designated as cash flow hedges:

- **$6,020 million notional amount** — the amount used to calculate the contractual cash flows exchanged under the swaps.
- **$(920) million fair value** — a liability; the swaps’ estimated termination value indicated Walmart would pay $920 million.

The swaps hedge currency exposure on forecast principal and interest payments for certain non-U.S.-denominated debt. (Form 10-K, Note 7, p. 69; Note 1, p. 61.)

All amounts are **$ millions**; a minus sign denotes a decrease. The 10-K reports the adoption in more than one way:

| Scope | Amount | What it measures |
|---|---:|---|
| Firmwide allowance | **−$587** | The adoption-date net decrease in the Firm’s allowance for credit losses. The allowance table shows this decrease in the allowance for loan losses. (Note 1, p. 173; Note 13, p. 258) |
| By loan portfolio | **Consumer, excluding credit card: −$489**; **Credit card: −$100**; **Wholesale: +$2**; **total: −$587** | The cumulative-effect adjustment to the allowance for loan losses by portfolio. No cumulative adjustment is shown for the allowance for lending-related commitments. (Note 13, p. 258; MD&A, p. 132) |
| Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) | **−$591** | A separately reported net decrease in CCB’s allowance for loan losses, driven by residential real estate and credit card. This is a segment-level figure, not an additional amount to add to the Firmwide portfolio breakdown. (CCB metrics, p. 70) |
| Retained earnings, TDR-specific | **+$446** | The after-tax increase in retained earnings from the TDR-guidance adoption, predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card. (Note 1, p. 173) |
| Retained earnings, equity-statement line | **+$449** | The statement of changes in equity’s “cumulative effect of change in accounting principles” line. Its footnote refers to both TDR and portfolio-layer hedging guidance adopted on January 1, so it is not identified as the TDR-only amount. (p. 169) |

Thus, the TDR-specific retained-earnings amount disclosed in Note 1 is **+$446 million after tax**; the **+$449 million** is the broader cumulative-effect line in the equity statement.

The 2021 Form 10-K names three projects:

- **Bacalhau Phase 1** in Brazil — funded in 2021; ExxonMobil also announced its final investment decision in June 2021 (pp. 18, 48).
- **North Field Production Sustainment Integrated Drilling and Looping** in Qatar — funded in 2021 (p. 19).
- **Jansz-Io Compression** in Australia — funded in 2021 (p. 20).

The 10-K gives two related descriptions of Huizhou’s capacity:

- **Ethylene:** **1.6 million metric tons per year**.
- **Polyethylene:** **1.7 million metric tons per year**.
- **Polypropylene:** **0.9 million metric tons per year**.

Those are the product-by-product figures in the year-end 2025 capacity table. Separately, the report says the complex’s **three polyethylene and two polypropylene lines together** have capacity of **over 2.5 million metric tons per year**. The table’s polyethylene and polypropylene figures total about **2.6 million**; the **1.6 million of ethylene is a separate capacity figure**, not part of that PE/PP combined total. (Form 10-K, pp. 21, 51.)

Excluding the gross-margin factors, Apple identifies these causes of quarter-to-quarter net-sales differences:

- **Seasonality:** Net sales have historically been higher in the first fiscal quarter, partly because of holiday demand.
- **Product and service launches:** Launches—and their timing—can affect sales. Indirect channels may be stocked with new products after a launch, while channel inventory of older products often declines ahead of a newer launch. Sales may also shift when customers or distributors anticipate an introduction.
- **Demand changes:** Lower-than-expected demand can affect sales; Apple notes that a significant share of net sales comes from one product, so a drop in demand for it could materially affect quarterly sales.
- **Unexpected disruptions:** Issues with new introductions, IT-system failures or network disruptions, or failures of logistics, component-supply, or manufacturing partners can affect net sales.

*Source: Apple fiscal 2023 Form 10-K, printed pp. 4 and 15.*

The filing says COVID-19’s initial effects on commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers were particularly severe. In the second quarter of 2020, Berkshire reassessed goodwill for certain reporting units, especially Precision Castparts (PCC). It considered airlines’ announcements about expected demand, employment and aircraft orders; manufacturers’ production cuts; and restructuring actions underway or being considered.

In light of those conditions, Berkshire judged it prudent to raise the discount rates and lower its previous long-term cash-flow forecasts used in the impairment review. It recorded $10.0 billion in pre-tax goodwill impairment and $638 million in indefinite-lived intangible-asset impairment, with approximately $10 billion related to PCC. Before the reassessment, PCC’s related goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets had carrying values of about $17 billion and $14 billion, respectively, largely arising from Berkshire’s 2016 acquisition of PCC. (2021 Form 10-K, p. K-63.)

Walmart reports two related fiscal 2025 figures:

- **$3,468 million** — the consolidated cash-flow statement’s total “Repayments of long-term debt,” shown as **$(3,468) million** because it is a financing cash outflow (p. 57).
- **$3,373 million** — Note 6’s total for **significant repayments of matured debt**, itemized as:
  - April 22, 2024: **$1,500 million**
  - July 8, 2024: **$990 million**
  - July 18, 2024: **$253 million** for a yen-denominated maturity
  - December 15, 2024: **$630 million** (p. 69)

The four Note 6 repayments sum to $3,373 million. Note 6 describes these as significant maturities; they are not an additional amount to add to the cash-flow total. The filing does not separately reconcile the $95 million difference between the two figures.

The filing attributes PCC’s 2021 revenue decline mainly to the pandemic’s impact on air travel and aircraft production. Reduced aircraft production reflected airline order delays and cancellations, as well as inventory-reduction initiatives across the industry. More broadly, Berkshire says the abrupt fall in air travel led to aircraft-build-rate cuts and customer destocking at extraordinary rates. It also identifies production delays in Boeing’s 737 MAX and 787 programs during that period as an additional adverse factor for PCC’s aerospace business. (Form 10-K, pp. K-12 and K-49.)

The 2025 Form 10-K gives **three 2026 commodity-price sensitivities** and **one pension-assumption sensitivity**:

| Change | Stated annual dollar effect |
|---|---|
| Brent crude: **$1 per barrel** | About **$700 million after tax** on Upstream earnings for consolidated and equity-company operations, excluding derivatives. Oil-linked LNG is about 10% of this sensitivity. |
| Henry Hub gas: **$0.10 per million metric British thermal units** | About **$90 million after tax** on the same Upstream earnings scope, excluding derivatives. |
| TTF gas: **$0.10 per million metric British thermal units** | About **$20 million after tax** on the same Upstream earnings scope, excluding derivatives; this sensitivity is primarily LNG sales. |
| Long-term expected return on plan assets: **a 0.5% reduction** | About **$150 million higher annual pension expense before tax**, worldwide. |

The commodity figures are approximate sensitivities, not forecasts; the filing notes that actual effects depend on factors such as trading, taxes, contract price lags, and production. It also says a 100-basis-point change in interest rates on debt would not be material, but gives no dollar estimate for that effect. (Market Risks, p. 62; Pension Benefits, p. 67.)
The increase reflected higher average First Republic-related deposits transferred from CCB to AWM in the fourth quarter of 2023.

The securities are investments in private companies without readily determinable fair values. NVIDIA uses the measurement alternative—cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for similar investments in the same issuer—but those adjustments can require unobservable inputs. The filing identifies volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and security-specific rights and obligations as valuation inputs. NVIDIA also assesses impairment quarterly using qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee’s operating performance and market trends. (Form 10-K, pp. 38, 66–67)

The Form 10-K says consumer credit performance, including net charge-offs, benefited from an improving macroeconomic environment. The decline was driven mainly by credit cards, where lower charge-offs and higher recoveries occurred as consumer cash balances remained elevated; greater residential real-estate net recoveries, reflecting further home-price-index improvement and more reversals of prior write-downs following prepayments in the low-rate environment; and fewer scored-auto charge-offs, supported by higher vehicle collateral values and elevated consumer cash balances. (2021 Form 10-K, pp. 110–116.)

Applying your filter, the 10-K gives these Flipkart-linked figures:

| Figure | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$3.2 billion** | Walmart said it received this in fiscal 2022, **primarily related to new equity funding** for its majority-owned Flipkart subsidiary. The funding reduced Walmart’s ownership from **approximately 83%** as of January 31, 2021, to **approximately 75%**. (pp. 43, 64) |
| **Approximately $2.2 billion** | Cash that could be accessed only through dividends or intercompany financing subject to approval by Flipkart’s minority shareholders; Walmart expected the cash to be used by Flipkart. (p. 42) |
| **$0.4 billion** | Fiscal 2020 impairment charges in Walmart International, consisting primarily of the write-off of the carrying value of Flipkart’s Jabong.com fashion trade name, as the business focused on Myntra.com. The filing does not give a separate Jabong-only impairment amount. (p. 71) |

I have not attributed broader Walmart or segment totals to Flipkart. For example, the filing says Flipkart share-based-compensation expense is included in the broader “Other” category, but does not break out a Flipkart-specific amount. (p. 64)

Beyond the purchase, valuation and pro forma disclosures, the 10-K gives these figures:

- **Share of ExxonMobil:** Pioneer represented **19% of consolidated assets** at December 31, 2024, and **4% of consolidated revenues** for 2024. ExxonMobil excluded Pioneer from its year-end internal-control assessment because it had been acquired during the year. *(Management’s Report on Internal Control, p. 73.)*
- **Actual post-acquisition results:** From **May 3 through December 31, 2024**, Pioneer contributed **$17.008 billion** in sales and other operating revenues and **$1.710 billion** in net income attributable to ExxonMobil. *(Note 21, p. 119.)*
- **Proved reserves:** ExxonMobil attributes about **2.3 billion oil-equivalent barrels (GOEB)** of its 2024 proved-reserve additions to the Pioneer acquisition. This is the acquisition-related addition, not a separate year-end Pioneer reserve total. *(Supplemental oil and gas information, p. 125.)*

For operating context, ExxonMobil reported **Permian production of about 1.185 million oil-equivalent barrels per day in 2024**, roughly **570,000 barrels per day above 2023**. That is combined Permian production, not a Pioneer-only figure. The MD&A also reported **$3.760 billion** of earnings growth from advantaged-volume growth, driven by Permian production—including both Pioneer and heritage Permian—and Guyana; it does not isolate Pioneer’s share. *(MD&A, pp. 47–48.)*

Pfizer says the increase mainly reflected the Arena, GBT and Biohaven acquisitions. It recorded IPR&D assets of $5.0 billion for Arena, $3.0 billion for GBT and $450 million for Biohaven. Partly offsetting those additions was a $200 million impairment of IPR&D acquired with Array, for an unapproved indication of symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy linked to a lamin A/C gene mutation. Pfizer says the Phase 3 trial reached futility at a pre-planned interim analysis (2022 Form 10-K, Notes 2A, 4 and 10).

Counting repeated company-wide discussions once, the 10-K identifies these fiscal 2024 improvements as benefiting from lapping fiscal 2023 items:

| Fiscal 2024 result | Lapped fiscal 2023 item |
|---|---|
| **Consolidated gross profit rate** rose 27 basis points. | Higher markdowns in the prior year, with the increase primarily driven by Walmart U.S. (pp. 38, 41). |
| **Consolidated operating expenses as a percentage of net sales** fell 60 basis points. | $3.3 billion in opioid-related legal-settlement charges and $0.8 billion in reorganization and restructuring charges for certain Walmart International businesses (pp. 38, 41). |
| **Consolidated operating income as a percentage of net sales** rose 83 basis points. | The 10-K says this was due to the factors above, including lapping the markdowns and charges (p. 38). |
| **Return on investment (ROI)** rose to 15.0% from 12.7%. | Opioid-settlement and reorganization/restructuring charges, all recorded in fiscal 2023 (p. 38). |
| **Walmart U.S. gross profit rate** rose 20 basis points. | Higher net markdowns incurred in the prior year (p. 42). |
| **Walmart International operating expenses as a percentage of segment net sales** fell 152 basis points. | Fiscal 2023 business reorganization and restructuring charges related to Flipkart and Massmart; higher sales also contributed (p. 43). |
| **Sam’s Club gross profit rate** rose 55 basis points. | Elevated markdowns in the prior year (p. 44). |

The segment discussions also report fiscal 2024 operating-income increases for Walmart U.S. ($1.5 billion), Walmart International ($1.9 billion) and Sam’s Club ($0.2 billion) as results of the factors discussed for those segments—including the lapping effects above (pp. 42–44).

The 10-K attributes the fiscal 2025 increases to:

- **Walmart overall:** Operating expenses rose from **20.4% to 20.7% of net sales** (+36 basis points). The filing cites higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan, increased marketing, and higher depreciation expenses (pp. 36, 39).
- **Walmart U.S.:** The ratio rose from **22.2% to 22.6%** (+44 basis points), due to increased marketing, higher variable pay from exceeding planned performance, and increased depreciation expenses (p. 40).
- **Sam’s Club U.S.:** The ratio rose from **10.8% to 11.2%** (+44 basis points), due to higher compensation-related expenses—including associate wage investments and higher variable pay from exceeding plan—and elevated technology spending (p. 42).

Walmart International’s ratio **decreased** from 18.6% to 18.5%, so it is not among the segments whose ratio rose (p. 41).

The filing cites **divestments, the expropriation of ExxonMobil’s Russian interests, and lower production entitlements as a result of higher prices** as the main offsets. It also says that easing government-mandated curtailments helped counter those effects. (MD&A, “Upstream Additional Information,” printed p. 52.)

The filing attributes the fiscal 2026 gross-profit-rate increases to:

- **Walmart overall (+8 basis points):** disciplined inventory management, primarily in Walmart U.S., and growth in higher-margin businesses globally.
- **Walmart U.S. (+22 basis points):** disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses.
- **Sam’s Club U.S. (+4 basis points):** operational efficiencies and higher fuel margins.

Walmart International’s rate declined, so it is not among the increases. (Form 10-K, pp. 35, 38–41.)

ExxonMobil describes a supply–demand squeeze: gasoline and diesel demand recovered to pre-pandemic levels, while pandemic-related refinery shutdowns, reduced investment, and broader capacity rationalization cut industry capacity. Supply-chain constraints added to the tight market, and low inventories and stronger demand boosted margins. The company also cites stronger trading and marketing margins as a contributor to its Energy Products margin improvement. *(MD&A, pp. 47, 53–54.)*

Pfizer says the increase was driven mainly by $8.0 billion of IPR&D recorded in its November 2025 acquisition of Metsera. This was partly offset by $3.9 billion of IPR&D impairments and by transfers out of IPR&D into developed technology rights: $600 million for Padcev and $590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna). The net increase was about $2.9 billion.

Pfizer says its 2025 Biopharma impairment charges primarily reflected changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts. The largest IPR&D impairments it identifies were $1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin, $820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib), and $820 million for osivelotor. (Note 10, p. 83; Note 4, p. 70.)
